common_name: Show 'n Tell Dahlia (Giant Red-Orange and Yellow Dinnerplate Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after soil has warmed and danger of frost has passed; give this AA-size dinnerplate plenty of elbow room and a sturdy stake set at planting time.

directions: Show 'n Tell produces enormous 8-10 inch informal decorative blooms with long, narrow petals that twist and curl at the tips, giving each flower a spiky, fireworks-like silhouette. The base color is a warm red-orange that fades toward sunny yellow near the petal tips, creating a two-tone glow that photographs especially well in late-day light. Plants build a bushy, upright framework of strong stems well suited to cutting, and benefit from disbudding side buds if exhibition-size blooms are the goal. Lift and store tubers after frost blackens the foliage in regions colder than zone 8.

common_name: Envy Dahlia (Rich Red Informal Decorative Dinnerplate Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after last frost; this 1965 introduction is a late-season bloomer, so gardeners in short-season climates should start tubers indoors a few weeks early.

directions: Envy is an heirloom informal decorative dahlia bred in 1965 that produces deep, saturated red blooms up to 11 inches across, rivaling the largest dinnerplate cultivars grown today. The broad, slightly twisted petals give the flower a full, substantial presence, though blooms often nod or face somewhat downward on their stems, so it reads best planted in a mixed border rather than staged as a single specimen. Plants grow to about four feet with a sturdy, branching habit, and stems should be staked early since the heavy flower heads can bend in wind and rain. It flowers relatively late in the season, typically around 120 days from planting, extending the garden's color into early fall.

common_name: Great Silence Dahlia (Peach-Rose and Gold Decorative Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally about 1 inch deep and 18 inches apart after last frost; slender dark stems make this variety a favorite for cutting gardens.

directions: Great Silence carries fully double decorative blooms about 4-5 inches across that appear a soft peach from a distance but reveal a subtle blend of rose-pink and gold up close, with each petal flushed lighter toward its base. The dark, slender flower stems contrast handsomely with the muted bloom color, making it a favorite among cut-flower growers seeking understated, painterly tones rather than bold primary colors. Plants form an upright, well-branched clump that holds its blooms well above the foliage without heavy staking. Deadhead regularly through summer to keep new buds coming until frost.

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after last frost; introduced in 2001, this ball dahlia is a prolific, reliable bloomer for cutting beds.

directions: Sylvia produces tightly packed, perfectly spherical ball-form blooms in hot tangerine-orange, each flower reaching about 4 inches wide on dark, near-black stems that set off the vivid color. First introduced in 2001, it quickly became popular for its abundance of blooms and reliable, uniform flower shape, making it a workhorse in cutting gardens and mixed borders alike. Plants reach roughly a yard tall on strong, upright stems that need little support even when loaded with flowers. Regular deadheading keeps this energetic bloomer producing from midsummer straight through to frost.

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after last frost; registered in 1955, this classic pompon is prized by wedding and specialty cut-flower growers for its tiny, perfectly round heads.

directions: Crossfield Ebony bears small, perfectly globular pompon blooms only 1.5-2 inches across, packed with tightly rolled petals in a deep burgundy-maroon so dark it reads as near-black in shade and glows garnet-red in bright sun. Registered in 1955 by W. Summerscales & Son of Crossfield Nursery in Yorkshire, England, it remains one of the most sought-after heirloom pompons for its color and flawless form. Plants grow upright to about three or four feet and produce blooms in abundance on wiry stems ideal for small arrangements and boutonnieres. Its diminutive, uniform flower heads hold up exceptionally well as cut flowers, making it a longtime favorite for wedding work.

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after last frost; this tall, heavy-flowered dinnerplate variety needs sturdy staking set in at planting time.

directions: Spartacus is a dramatic informal decorative dinnerplate dahlia with huge, deeply saturated blooms 8-10 inches wide that blend plum, scarlet, and near-black tones into a velvety black-crimson that deepens further as flowers age. The wide, ruffled petals have a slight wave along their edges, giving each bloom a bold, dynamic texture rather than a flat face. Plants are vigorous and tall, often exceeding four feet, with thick stems capable of supporting the enormous flower heads, though staking is still recommended in exposed sites. Its dramatic coloring and imposing size make it a standout back-of-border plant and a striking focal bloom in cut arrangements.

common_name: Moonfire Dahlia (Single Golden-Orange Bloom over Near-Black Foliage)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after last frost; the dark bronze-purple foliage emerges early and provides garden interest before bloom time.

directions: Moonfire pairs single, open-faced blooms about 3 inches across in golden orange, blushed with orange-red toward the center, with a dark chocolate-brown central disc flecked by bright golden stamens. Its deeply cut foliage emerges purple-black and holds that dark coloring all season, echoing the dark-leaved Bishop series but with a distinct single flower form rather than a double peony shape. Plants form a compact, well-branched mound that stays under three feet, making it useful for the front of borders or container plantings where the foliage contrast can be appreciated up close. It was originally raised in the Netherlands and later named in the UK after being mistakenly supplied to a nursery as an unlabeled seedling.
